repos.title: Attention Is All You Need
repos.paper_summary:
The Transformer is a sequence transduction model that replaces recurrent and convolutional layers with multi-head self-attention. The architecture consists of six encoder and six decoder stacks, each containing sub-layers for scaled dot-product attention and position-wise feed-forward networks. Positional information is injected via fixed sinusoidal encodings added to token embeddings.

On the WMT 2014 English-to-German task, the large variant achieves 28.4 BLEU, exceeding previous best ensembles by over 2.0 BLEU. For English-to-French, it reaches 41.8 BLEU after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs. A base configuration requires only 12 hours of training on the same hardware. The model also generalizes to English constituency parsing, achieving 92.7 F1 in a semi-supervised setting. Limitations include quadratic computational complexity relative to sequence length and reliance on beam search during inference.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Recurrent models process positions sequentially, which limits parallelization; the authors propose the Transformer, which uses only attention.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Prior convolutional models need operations that grow with distance between positions; the Transformer reduces this to a constant number.

digest_headlines.heading: Model Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: The model stacks six encoder and decoder layers built on scaled dot-product and multi-head attention, with sinusoidal positional encodings.

digest_headlines.heading: Why Self-Attention
digest_headlines.headline: Self-attention needs a constant number of sequential operations and a constant maximum path length, versus linear for recurrent layers.

digest_headlines.heading: Training
digest_headlines.headline: Models trained on WMT 2014 data with Adam and a warmup learning-rate schedule, using dropout and label smoothing.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: The big Transformer scores 28.4 BLEU on English-to-German, above prior results including ensembles, and generalizes to parsing.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude the Transformer trains faster than recurrent or convolutional models and plan to extend it to other modalities.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix shows layer-5 encoder attention heads tracking long-distance verb dependencies, anaphora, and sentence structure.

repos.title: CAVEWOMAN: How Large Language Models Behave Under Linguistic Input and Output Compression
repos.paper_summary:
Cavewoman is a two-channel evaluation protocol that measures task accuracy, realized per-item cost, and reference-text agreement for large language models under linguistic compression. The method applies deterministic part-of-speech filters to user prompts (input compression) or constrains model responses via system prompts (output compression) across five reduction levels. It evaluates eight models on five datasets, including GSM8K and MMLU-STEM, totaling 11,465 items per model.

Output compression reduces realized cost by 1.4–2.4× on most API models and up to 3× in the best case, while input compression increases net cost by approximately 1.15× on average due to compensatory output expansion. Under output compression, 51.9% of generations from non-reasoning models are correct but their surface text no longer entails the model’s unconstrained baseline; this rate rises to 80.4% under length-controlled re-scoring. The paper notes that robustness to compression varies widely across models and is not predicted by parameter count or unconstrained accuracy. Limitations include the use of greedy decoding only, short structured answers that may not generalize to long-form generation, and the fact that NLI judges measure surface-text divergence rather than propositional content.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Accuracy at a reduced token count cannot separate realized cost from prompt reduction, so Cavewoman scores both channels on three axes.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior compression methods each reduce one channel and report accuracy at a token budget, and none checks reference-text agreement.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Cavewoman holds the model and question fixed and applies five reduction levels to either the prompt or the response.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Output compression lowers realized cost on most API models while input compression raises it, and correct answers still diverge from reference text.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Single-axis evaluation is underdetermined, because cost, accuracy and reference agreement dissociate and a composite metric can mis-rank methods.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Candidates should be ranked at their deployment constraint level, since output-compression tolerance is not predicted by parameter count or unconstrained accuracy.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists pricing, dataset statistics, inference configuration, token and cost accounting, constraint specifications, and released artifacts.

repos.title: OpenDataLab: Empowering General Artificial Intelligence with Open Datasets
repos.paper_summary: OpenDataLab is an open data platform and toolchain that standardizes heterogeneous AI datasets using a new specification called Data Set Description Language (DSDL). The system integrates over 6,500 datasets totaling more than 80 TB, including 6 billion images, 1 trillion tokens, and 20,000 hours of audio. DSDL defines a unified syntax for multimodal data representation, allowing users to merge datasets from different sources through a Python SDK or configuration files without manual format alignment. The platform provides a CLI, SDK, and labeling tools (`LabelU` for computer vision tasks and `LabelLLM` for dialogue data) to support the full workflow from download to training. The authors report that this integrated approach improves data preparation efficiency by 30%. A limitation is that the 30% efficiency gain is stated as a general claim without a detailed experimental protocol or baseline comparison in the text. Additionally, while DSDL aims for universality, it currently supports only over 100 standardized datasets, leaving many available formats unconverted.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: OpenDataLab is presented as a five-layer architecture that aims to remove barriers between datasets and processing tools.

digest_headlines.heading: Open Datasets
digest_headlines.headline: OpenDataLab hosts over 6,500 open datasets and records source and license metadata for them.

digest_headlines.heading: Data Set Description Language (DSDL)
digest_headlines.headline: DSDL is a dataset description language designed for universality, portability and extensibility.

digest_headlines.heading: Open Data Platform and Data Toolkits
digest_headlines.headline: The platform adds search, preview, free hosting and download, command-line and Python access, and two labeling tools.

digest_headlines.heading: Use Case
digest_headlines.headline: A worked object detection example merges two datasets with DSDL instead of hand-written alignment code.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: A self-assessed comparison table rates OpenDataLab strong on most dimensions, against weaker ratings for rival platforms.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors report a 30% gain in data preparation efficiency, with no experiment shown in the text.

repos.title: OpenHands: An Open Platform for AI Software Developers as Generalist Agents
repos.paper_summary: OpenHands is an open-source platform for building and evaluating AI agents that act on the world by writing code, running shell commands, and browsing the web. Its main components are an event stream that records actions and observations, a Docker-sandboxed runtime with a bash shell, an IPython server, and a Chromium browser, an AgentSkills library of editing and document-parsing tools, and an AgentHub of community agents, including the default CodeAct agent. Agents can delegate subtasks to other agents, and users can add agents or new Docker images. The evaluation framework covers 15 benchmarks, including SWE-Bench, HumanEvalFix, BIRD, and WebArena. The paper reports results across these tasks, but the text provided here does not include the per-benchmark scores, so this summary cannot state them. The platform is released under the MIT license and has 32K GitHub stars and more than 2.1K contributions from over 188 contributors. The paper acknowledges that building agents that are safe and reliable remains an open challenge, which its appendix covers.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: OpenHands is a community platform for building agents that write code, use a shell, and browse the web.

digest_headlines.heading: OpenHands Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: Agents are defined by a step function over an event stream, and actions run in a Docker sandbox that returns observations.

digest_headlines.heading: AgentHub: A Hub of Community-Contributed Agents
digest_headlines.headline: The AgentHub ships a default CodeAct agent, a browsing agent, a graph-based agent, and a template for micro agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Across 15 benchmarks, the CodeActAgent resolves 26% of software engineering issues and fixes 79.3% of Python bugs.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: OpenHands is presented as a community platform that accelerates research and applications of agentic AI systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers limitations, ethics, related work, the graphical interface, integration tests, runtime image building, graduate-level benchmark results, prompts, skills, and BrowserGym actions.

repos.title: LlamaFactory: Unified Efficient Fine-Tuning of 100+ Language Models
repos.paper_summary:
LlamaFactory is a unified framework integrating efficient fine-tuning methods to adapt over 100 large language models without custom code. It comprises three modules: a Model Loader attaching adapters like LoRA, QLoRA, and GaLore; a Data Worker standardizing dataset formats; and a Trainer supporting pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, and DPO. A key feature is model-sharing RLHF, which uses dynamic adapter switching to run the full pipeline on a single pre-trained model. The web interface LlamaBoard allows users to configure experiments and monitor training in real time.

The authors validate the framework on an NVIDIA A100 GPU using Gemma-2B, Llama2-7B, and Llama2-13B. On a corpus of roughly 400K tokens from PubMed abstracts, 4-bit QLoRA reduces peak memory to 5.21 GB for Gemma-2B compared to 17.06 GB for full tuning, while LoRA achieves a throughput of 3521 tokens/s. In downstream text generation tasks with 2,000 training examples, LoRA and QLoRA generally match or exceed full-tuning ROUGE scores across eight instruction-tuned models. Limitations include the requirement for adapter-based methods when using quantized weights and the fact that full-tuning Llama2-13B exceeds the 40GB memory limit of the test hardware.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-tuning large language models is costly, so LlamaFactory unifies efficient fine-tuning methods in one framework.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing fine-tuning frameworks support fewer efficient methods than LlamaFactory, as its feature comparison shows.

digest_headlines.heading: Efficient Fine-Tuning Techniques
digest_headlines.headline: The paper groups efficient fine-tuning into optimization methods, such as LoRA, and computation methods, such as flash attention.

digest_headlines.heading: LlamaFactory Framework
digest_headlines.headline: LlamaFactory has three modules, Model Loader, Data Worker and Trainer, with a web interface called LlamaBoard.

digest_headlines.heading: Empirical Study
digest_headlines.headline: Across tested models, quantized low-rank adaptation used the least memory and low-rank adaptation scored best on most generation tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Future work targets more modalities, parallel training strategies and stronger methods for conversational models.

digest_headlines.heading: Broader Impact and Responsible Use
digest_headlines.headline: The authors expect the framework to benefit open-source communities, and require users to follow model licenses.

repos.title: ResearchStudio-Reel: Automate the Last Mile of Research from Paper to Poster, Video, and Blog
repos.paper_summary:
ResearchStudio-Reel is a set of five skills, runnable in Claude Code and Codex, that turns one paper PDF into an editable PowerPoint poster, a narrated talk video with a PowerPoint deck, and a bilingual Word blog. A shared extractor, Paper2Assets, builds one bundle of text, cleaned figures, metadata, and section IDs that all three generators read, so none of them re-parses the PDF. Paper2Poster uses a measured-fill loop that scores each section's fill ratio, edits sections until they fall between 0.90 and 0.98, and requires figures to fill at least 90% of their card. Paper2Reel then links poster regions, video segments, and blog passages in one HTML viewer.

On the 100-paper Paper2Poster benchmark, the Claude Code configuration has the best scores among automated systems on all three aesthetic sub-criteria and the best or tied-best on two of three information sub-criteria. Under two VLM judges, its average aesthetic score is 3.56 versus 3.03 for the authors' posters, and it wins overall on 74 and 95 of the 100 papers.

The paper states that its evaluative, generative, and architectural limits remain to be studied. The provided text reports no quantitative evaluation for the video or blog artifacts.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Paper-to-poster, video, and blog tools mostly stay artifact-specific, so the paper proposes an editable, linked workspace for all three.

digest_headlines.heading: Skills
digest_headlines.headline: Five skills share one extracted bundle, with three generators feeding a single interactive viewer that keeps sections aligned.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On the 100-paper benchmark, the Claude Code configuration scores 3.56 on aesthetics against the authors' 3.03.

digest_headlines.heading: Applications
digest_headlines.headline: Three intended users, an individual author, a lab, and a course, would run the same pipeline at different cadences.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Prior paper-to-poster, video, and blog systems each target one output, while this work binds editable artifacts into one linked viewer.

digest_headlines.heading: Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Evaluation relies on proxy measures, and the pipeline cannot yet create new method or overview diagrams.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Editable, linked artifacts are delivered, with posters above the authors' own on aesthetics under two judges.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists failure modes, scope limits, ethics, reproducibility, per-judge scores, comparisons, a gallery, and the baseline prompt.

repos.title: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models
repos.paper_summary: Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) train diffusion models in the latent space of pretrained autoencoders to reduce computational costs while preserving image quality. The method first trains an autoencoder using perceptual and adversarial losses to create a compressed representation, then applies a UNet-based diffusion model to this space. Cross-attention layers allow conditioning on text, bounding boxes, or semantic maps. On ImageNet class-conditional synthesis, the 400M parameter LDM-4-G achieves a FID of 3.60 and IS of 247.67 with classifier-free guidance, outperforming ADM-G (FID 4.59) with fewer parameters. For text-to-image generation on MS-COCO, the 1.45B parameter LDM-KL-8-G reaches a FID of 12.63 and IS of 30.29, comparable to larger autoregressive baselines. In super-resolution, LDM-SR attains a FID of 2.8 and generates 4 samples per second on an A100 GPU, compared to SR3’s FID of 5.2. Limitations include slower sequential sampling than GANs and potential quality loss in pixel-accurate tasks due to autoencoder compression.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Pixel-space diffusion models are costly to train and sample, so the paper moves them into a learned latent space.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier generative approaches trade off sample quality, speed and resolution, and pixel-space diffusion models are costly to optimize and sample.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Latent diffusion models train a UNet on latents from a perceptual autoencoder, and add cross-attention for conditioning inputs such as text.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Latent models with downsampling factors 4 to 8 reach much lower Fréchet inception distance (FID) than pixel-based diffusion, a gap of 38 after 2M steps.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations & Societal Impact
digest_headlines.headline: Latent models still sample more slowly than GANs, and autoencoder reconstruction can limit tasks that need fine pixel accuracy.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude that latent diffusion improves training and sampling efficiency without degrading quality across several conditional tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers the changelog, the diffusion objective derivation, guidance, extra results, compute comparisons and autoencoder training details.

repos.title: DocLayNet: A Large Human-Annotated Dataset for Document-Layout Analysis
repos.paper_summary:
DocLayNet is a publicly available dataset of 80,863 human-annotated PDF pages designed for document layout analysis. The annotations consist of labeled bounding boxes across 11 classes (e.g., Text, Table, Formula) in COCO format. Unlike previous datasets derived from scientific repositories, DocLayNet includes diverse sources such as financial reports and manuals to capture layout variability. A subset of pages contains double or triple annotations to measure inter-annotator agreement.

Baseline experiments using Mask R-CNN, Faster R-CNN, and YOLOv5 show that model performance lags behind human annotation by approximately 10% in mAP@0.5–0.95. Specifically, the best-performing YOLOv5x6 achieves an overall mAP of 76.8%, compared to the human agreement range of 82–83%. A data ablation study indicates that model accuracy plateaus at 80% of the dataset size. Additionally, splitting data on document boundaries rather than individual pages reduces mAP by roughly 10 points, highlighting the risk of overestimation with page-wise splits. Models trained on DocLayNet demonstrate more consistent cross-dataset performance than those trained on PubLayNet or DocBank.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing layout datasets come from scientific repositories, so DocLayNet adds human-annotated pages with wider layout variety.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior layout analysis moved from rule-based methods to object detection, and newer text-plus-image models lack a shared data format.

digest_headlines.heading: The DocLayNet Dataset
digest_headlines.headline: DocLayNet contains 80863 pages from six document categories, with 11 labels and pre-defined splits that keep documents whole.

digest_headlines.heading: Annotation Campaign
digest_headlines.headline: Four-phase human annotation under a guideline over 100 pages long improved consistency, though 8 of 40 annotators did not pass.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Baseline detectors trail human agreement by 6 to 10%, and random page-wise splits inflate scores by about 10%.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: DocLayNet supplies human reference metrics and models that transfer better across datasets, yet a gap to humans remains.

repos.title: Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory
repos.paper_summary: Mem0 is a memory system for LLM agents that extracts, consolidates, and retrieves salient facts from ongoing conversations. Mem0g is a variant that stores those facts as a directed labeled graph of entities and relations. Mem0 runs an extraction phase, which prompts an LLM with a conversation summary, recent messages, and a new message pair to produce candidate facts, and an update phase, which retrieves similar stored memories and has the LLM choose ADD, UPDATE, DELETE, or NOOP through a tool call. On the LOCOMO benchmark, overall LLM-as-a-Judge (J) scores are 66.88% for Mem0 and 68.44% for Mem0g, compared with 60.97% for the best RAG setting and 72.90% for full-context prompting. Mem0 has a p95 total latency of 1.440 s, versus 17.117 s for full-context. Its memory store averages about 7k tokens per conversation, versus about 26k tokens for raw context and over 600k for Zep. Limitations: full-context scores highest on J, Zep leads on open-domain questions, and Mem0g does not improve multi-hop results.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fixed context windows make AI agents forget user facts across sessions, so the paper proposes persistent memory systems, Mem0 and a graph-based variant.

digest_headlines.heading: Proposed Methods
digest_headlines.headline: Mem0 extracts candidate facts from message pairs and updates memory through add, update, delete or skip decisions; the graph variant stores entities and relations.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: The paper tests on the LOCOMO benchmark, scoring answers with lexical overlap metrics and LLM-as-a-Judge against six baseline categories.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation Results, Analysis and Discussion.
digest_headlines.headline: Mem0 leads single-hop and multi-hop questions, the graph variant leads temporal questions, and Zep leads open-domain questions among compared systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion claims a balance of accuracy and latency, and names graph operation overhead and non-conversational domains as future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the LLM-as-a-Judge prompt source, has an empty algorithm section, and describes the LoCoMo, ReadAgent, MemoryBank, MemGPT and A-Mem baselines.
